questions.stem: What is the resting potential of a neurone approximately equal to?

options.text: -70 mV
0 mV
+70 mV
+40 mV

questions.explanation: The resting potential is approximately -70 mV, meaning the inside of the neurone is negatively charged relative to the outside. This is maintained by the sodium-potassium pump and the distribution of ions across the membrane.

questions.stem: What does the sodium-potassium pump do?

options.text: Pumps equal numbers of sodium and potassium ions
Pumps 3 sodium ions out and 2 potassium ions in
Pumps 3 sodium ions in and 2 potassium ions out
Allows sodium and potassium to diffuse freely

questions.explanation: The sodium-potassium pump actively transports 3 Na+ ions out of the cell for every 2 K+ ions pumped in. This uses ATP and creates the uneven ion distribution needed to maintain the negative resting potential.

questions.stem: During an action potential, what happens first when the threshold is reached?

options.text: Potassium channels open and K+ rushes out
The sodium-potassium pump speeds up
Sodium channels open and Na+ rushes in
The membrane becomes more negative

questions.explanation: When the threshold potential is reached, voltage-gated sodium channels open rapidly, allowing Na+ ions to rush into the cell. This causes depolarisation, making the inside of the cell positively charged (up to about +40 mV).

questions.stem: What is the importance of the refractory period?

options.text: It allows the neurone to fire continuously without stopping
It prevents the neurone from ever firing again
It speeds up the rate of impulse transmission
It ensures impulses travel in one direction only along the axon

questions.explanation: During the refractory period, the section of membrane that has just fired cannot generate another action potential immediately. This ensures the impulse can only travel forwards along the axon, preventing it from travelling backwards.

questions.stem: Which factor increases the speed of nerve impulse transmission?

options.text: The absence of a myelin sheath
The presence of a myelin sheath
A thinner axon diameter
A lower body temperature

questions.explanation: The myelin sheath speeds up impulse transmission by enabling saltatory conduction, where the impulse jumps between nodes of Ranvier. A wider axon diameter and higher temperature also increase speed.

questions.stem: What does the 'all-or-nothing' principle of nerve impulses mean?

options.text: Only motor neurones can generate action potentials
All neurones fire at the same time
The impulse gets stronger as it travels along the axon
A neurone either fires a full action potential or does not fire at all

questions.explanation: The all-or-nothing principle means that if the threshold is reached, a full action potential is generated; if the threshold is not reached, no impulse occurs. The size of the action potential is always the same regardless of stimulus strength.

questions.stem: What type of conduction occurs when impulses jump along a myelinated axon from node to node?

options.text: Synaptic transmission
Passive conduction
Continuous conduction
Saltatory conduction

questions.explanation: Saltatory conduction occurs in myelinated neurones, where the impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next. This is much faster than continuous conduction in unmyelinated neurones, where the impulse must travel along every part of the membrane.
